back: Collects usage/configuration/dependency data from on-premises servers (agentless or agent-based) to inform migration planning — feeds data into Migration Hub so you know what you're migrating and how systems depend on each other before you move them.

AWS's recommended lift-and-shift (rehost) tool — continuously replicates on-premises or other-cloud servers to AWS, allowing low-downtime cutover; it has effectively replaced the legacy Server Migration Service (SMS) as the current exam-relevant rehosting tool.

Migrates databases to AWS (homogeneous or heterogeneous, e.g. Oracle to Aurora) with minimal downtime via continuous replication (CDC).

For heterogeneous migrations (different source/target engines), DMS is almost always paired with the Schema Conversion Tool (SCT), which converts the schema/code first — DMS alone only migrates data, not schema logic like stored procedures.

Automates and accelerates large-scale, one-time or recurring data transfer between on-premises storage (NFS/SMB) and S3/EFS/FSx, or between AWS storage services, with built-in encryption, scheduling, and validation — much faster than manual scripted transfers over the same links.

Single console to track the progress of migrations happening across multiple AWS and partner migration tools (Application Discovery Service, DMS, MGN, etc.) — a tracking/visibility layer, not a migration engine itself.

Converts database schema and code (stored procedures, views, functions) from one engine to another (e.g. Oracle to PostgreSQL) ahead of a heterogeneous migration.

Always paired with DMS in exam scenarios: SCT converts the schema/code, DMS migrates the actual data.

Physical devices for offline bulk data transfer and edge computing: Snowcone (smallest, portable, includes some compute), Snowball Edge (larger, storage- or compute-optimized, can run EC2/Lambda at the edge), and Snowmobile (exabyte-scale, a literal shipping container on a truck, now largely superseded by high-count Snowball Edge fleets).

Fully managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints backed directly by S3 or EFS, letting partners/legacy systems keep using familiar file-transfer protocols while data lands natively in AWS storage — avoids needing to stand up and maintain your own FTP servers.

front: When is a Snow Family device the right answer on the exam?
back: When transferring the data over the network would take weeks or months — a function of data size vs. available bandwidth — a physical Snow device beats network transfer.

The framework for deciding how to move a given workload to AWS, roughly ordered from least to most re-engineering effort:

  • Retire — turn it off; no longer needed.
  • Retain — keep it on-premises for now (e.g. not ready, or must stay for compliance).
  • Rehost — 'lift and shift'; move as-is, typically via AWS Application Migration Service (MGN).
  • Replatform — 'lift, tinker, and shift'; a few targeted optimizations (e.g. moving to a managed database) without changing the core architecture.
  • Repurchase — switch to a different product, usually a SaaS replacement (e.g. moving a self-hosted CRM to Salesforce).
  • Refactor / Re-architect — redesign the application to be cloud-native, usually to add capabilities hard to achieve in the current architecture.

Every migration tool in this deck (DMS, MGN, SCT, DataSync) implements one specific R — this framework is the strategic layer above them.

Purpose-built service for migrating mainframe workloads (e.g. COBOL batch applications) to AWS, offering automated tooling to convert and refactor existing mainframe code and data rather than requiring a full ground-up rewrite of business logic that's often decades old and poorly documented.

Exam trigger: 'migrate a critical mainframe application while preserving existing business logic, without a full rewrite' — distinct from AWS Application Migration Service (MGN), which rehosts standard x86 servers/VMs as-is and isn't built for specialized mainframe architectures.

Collects on-premises server inventory and actual utilization data to build a data-driven, right-sized cost comparison between current infrastructure spend and a projected AWS environment — the tool for building the pre-migration business case, before any migration tooling is chosen.

Distinct from AWS Application Discovery Service (dependency mapping for migration wave planning) and the AWS Pricing Calculator (manual cost estimates for resources you specify yourself, with no on-premises data collection) — Migration Evaluator's whole point is turning real utilization data into a defensible cost projection.

A guided deployment wizard that sizes, provisions, and configures AWS infrastructure for specific named enterprise workloads (e.g. SAP, Microsoft SQL Server Always On, Active Directory) according to that workload's own vendor best practices — instead of manually researching and assembling the right EC2 instances, storage, and networking by hand.

Exam trigger: 'deploy [SAP / a specific enterprise workload] on AWS following that vendor's official best-practice architecture' without hand-building it from general EC2 guidance.

Analyzes an existing running Java or .NET application on a server, automatically containerizes it (generating the Dockerfile and container image), and produces the matching ECS/EKS deployment artifacts (task definitions, CloudFormation templates) — without a team manually rewriting Dockerfiles or restructuring the application by hand.

Exam distinction: App2Container containerizes an application in place; AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) instead rehosts an entire server/VM as-is onto EC2 and doesn't containerize anything.

An incremental application modernization pattern: a routing layer (typically API Gateway or an ALB) sits in front of both a legacy monolith and a growing set of new microservices, gradually directing specific paths/endpoints to new services as they're built, while the monolith keeps serving everything not yet migrated — until it's fully replaced and can be retired.

Exam trigger: 'modernize a business-critical monolith without a risky big-bang cutover, building new functionality as microservices from day one' — the alternative to a full rewrite-and-replace-at-once approach.

Runs the actual VMware stack (vSphere, NSX, vSAN) on AWS-owned, AWS-hosted infrastructure — lets a company move an existing VMware environment to AWS as-is, keeping its existing VMware-specific tooling, configurations, and staff skills intact, rather than reconfiguring every workload's networking/storage to native AWS services up front.

Exam trigger: a large VMware estate under time pressure (e.g. a fixed data-center-exit deadline) that isn't ready to redesign around native AWS services yet, but wants to modernize individual applications later at its own pace.
